n: David builds homes for himself in Jerusalem, but he also prepares a special tent for the ark. Making a place for God is part of building his kingdom.
David has learned from Uzza’s death: only Levites may carry the ark, because God chose them for that service.

f.w: None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites

n: Once again David gathers all Israel to Jerusalem to bring the ark to the place he has prepared.

f.g: To its appointed place—the tent in the city of David.

n: This time David calls the priests and Levites first.
The Levite families are organized under their leaders, beginning with the Kohathites, who were originally assigned to carry the holiest objects.
The Merarites, led by Asaiah, number 220.
The Gershonites, led by Joel, number 130.
Elizaphan’s clan, a branch of the Kohathites, sends 200.

f.g: A Kohathite leader in Moses’ day (Numbers 3:30).

n: Hebron’s clan, another Kohathite branch, sends eighty.
Uzziel’s clan, the last of six family groups, sends 112. In all, 862 Levites take part.
David summons both chief priests, Zadok and Abiathar, along with the six Levite leaders.
He tells them to sanctify themselves—to become ritually and spiritually prepared—before carrying the ark.

f.g: Make yourselves holy through cleansing rituals and devotion.

n: David humbly admits the earlier failure: because we did not seek God “after the due order,” He broke out against us. God’s work must be done in God’s way.

f.g: According to the proper, prescribed pattern.

n: The priests and Levites prepare themselves as instructed.
This time the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders with poles, exactly as Moses commanded—no cart.

f.g: With the carrying poles in place.

n: David also organizes musicians to accompany the ark with joyful song and instruments.

f.w: lifting up the voice with joy

n: Three master musicians are appointed—Heman, Asaph and Ethan—one from each branch of Levi.

f.g: Kushaiah is called Kishi in 1 Chronicles 6:44.

n: Assistant musicians and gatekeepers of the second rank are named, including Obed-edom, in whose house the ark had rested.
The three leaders play bronze cymbals, probably to keep the rhythm and signal the start of songs.
A second group plays lyres set to “Alamoth.”

f.g: A musical term, possibly meaning “young women,” i.e., a higher register or soprano voices.

n: A third group plays harps set to “the Sheminith” to lead the music.

f.g: A musical term meaning “the eighth,” possibly a lower octave or an eight-stringed instrument.
To lead or direct the music.

n: Chenaniah, a skilled musician, directs the singing.

f.g: He was in charge of the music; some read “in charge of the carrying.”

n: Berechiah and Elkanah guard the ark.

f.g: Guards protecting the ark from improper approach.

n: Priests blow trumpets before the ark, as in Israel’s great processions, and more doorkeepers stand guard.
David, the elders and the army commanders joyfully bring the ark from Obed-edom’s house.
When it is clear that God is helping the Levites carry the ark safely, they offer seven bulls and seven rams in thanksgiving.

f.g: In contrast to the earlier disaster, God now blesses their obedient effort.

n: David wears a fine linen robe and a linen ephod—simple priestly-style clothing—joining in worship humbly rather than in royal splendor.

f.g: A simple linen garment worn in sacred service.

n: All Israel brings up the ark with shouts and music. It is one of the most joyful celebrations in the Old Testament.
But Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s wife, watches from a window and despises David for dancing. Her contempt contrasts with David’s wholehearted joy before the Lord.

f.g: Looked down on him with scorn.
